summary:
When a river floods, clouds usually cover the area, and optical satellites can’t see the water when responders need it most. Under the Clouds uses satellite radar, which sees through clouds and at night, to map new flood water and show which roads and villages are affected.

We trained a U-Net deep learning model on Sentinel-1 radar to recognise water (IoU 0.687 on 90 benchmark test scenes, better than the best simple threshold on all 11 flood events in the dataset). We compare a radar image from before the flood with one from during it, clean out false alarms, and overlay OpenStreetMap roads and places.

We applied it to the Loukkos River floods around Ksar El Kebir, Morocco (January–February 2026): an estimated 51.2 km² of new water, 22.9 km of road in flooded areas and 35 places within 500 m. Results are shown on an interactive map that starts from a spinning Earth made of NASA imagery.

We also tested NASA-ISRO’s new NISAR L-band radar on a real flood in Mozambique. We report our limits openly: the Moroccan numbers are model estimates, and two independent checks there show where the model falls short.
details:
What does it do?

Under the Clouds maps floods through clouds. It takes two satellite radar images of the same place, one before a flood and one during it, and turns them into a map of new flood water and a list of the roads and villages to check first. Floods come with clouds, so normal satellite photos are often blind when they’re needed most. Radar sends its own signal and sees through clouds, day and night. The result is shown on a web map that anyone can open with a link, with no radar knowledge needed.

How does it work?

Radar data. We order Sentinel-1 radar images through NASA’s ASF DAAC and process them with ASF HyP3 (radiometric terrain correction, 30 m pixels), which runs in the cloud for free.

Water detection. A U-Net deep learning model with a ResNet-34 encoder (24.4 million parameters) reads the two radar polarizations (VV and VH) and labels every pixel as water or not water. It was trained on the Sen1Floods11 dataset. On 90 test scenes it reaches IoU 0.687, against 0.530 for the best simple threshold (a single tuned VH threshold). On a flood it never saw in training (Bolivia) it reaches 0.601, against 0.586 for the best threshold on that flood (a simple per-scene threshold). Scored flood by flood in 11 countries, it beats the tuned VH threshold on every one. The weakest is Pakistan (IoU 0.27), and we show it openly.

Change detection. New flood water is water during the flood that wasn’t there before. Rivers, lakes and reservoirs appear in both images, so they aren’t counted.

Clean-up. Calm sea looks like flood water in radar. We remove the sea and a 1 km coastal strip with a land mask, then remove thin shapes (shifting river banks) and very small blobs.

Impact. We overlay OpenStreetMap roads and places and keep those touching the new water.

Interface. A spinning Earth made from NASA Blue Marble, Black Marble and the real clouds of 8 February 2026 (via NASA GIBS). Clicking the marker opens a flat map with a before/after slider, flood and impact layers, and NASA basemaps. A cloud test puts NASA’s optical image of the flood day, covered in cloud, next to our radar flood map, with a clear-sky date and a link to NASA Worldview so anyone can check it. A “Radar change” layer shows any change in radar brightness between the two dates. A button downloads a situation report for responders as a spreadsheet. A time machine plays the model’s water over 11 Sentinel-1 passes (22 December 2025 to 20 February 2026), showing the flood rising and falling. Full-screen Evidence and NISAR pages show every check we ran, and a 60-second guided tour walks through the story. For the 11 benchmark floods, a slider compares the model’s water with the hand-labelled water.

Case study: the Loukkos River floods, Morocco

From late January 2026, heavy rain and releases from the Oued Al Makhazine dam (more than 372 million m³ of water) flooded the Loukkos plain around Ksar El Kebir. More than 140,000 people were evacuated, according to news reports. Using Sentinel-1 images from 21 January and 8 February 2026, our model estimates 51.2 km² of new flood water, 22.9 km of road in flooded areas (60 segments) and 35 places within 500 m. These are model estimates, not measured values.

What benefits does it have?

It works under full cloud cover and at night. It uses only free, global data: Sentinel-1, NISAR, OpenStreetMap and Natural Earth cover the whole planet, so the same pipeline can run on any flood with one image before and one during. Once the radar images are processed (about an hour with HyP3), the analysis takes minutes. Most importantly, it doesn’t stop at a water map: it answers the questions responders actually ask, “Which roads are under water?” and “Which villages may be cut off?”

What is the intended impact?

Faster, better-targeted flood response, especially in places without their own mapping teams. A civil protection office could open the map, see the affected roads and villages, and download a list to plan where to send help first. The approach could also sit on top of existing global water products: they say where water is, and our impact layer says what it touches.

How is the project creative?

Radar to see under the clouds, and a cloud test that shows it in one picture: cloud on one side, the flood on the other.

From the whole Earth to one road: the interface starts from a spinning globe of real NASA imagery and zooms down to individual roads and villages.

A time machine that shows the flood rising to a peak on 8 February and falling again, from the model’s water on 11 radar passes.

NASA-ISRO NISAR, the newest radar. NISAR has no data over Ksar El Kebir before June 2026, so it couldn’t see this flood. We tested it anyway. On a NISAR image of Ksar El Kebir (25 October 2026), our Sentinel-1 model found nothing (IoU 0.00), because in L-band water is only about 4 dB darker than land in HV, against about 13 dB in Sentinel-1. Without retraining, we fed HH in place of VV, built a synthetic VH from HH, and shifted HH to the Sentinel-1 brightness level. That reached IoU 0.63 against OpenStreetMap water (one scene, mostly permanent water).

A real NISAR flood test. We then found a flood NISAR did see: the Limpopo floods in Mozambique, January 2026 (before 5 January, during 17 January). We compared with the Copernicus EMS expert flood map of 18 January. The settings came from Ksar El Kebir, and the brightness shift was computed from the before image only, so nothing was tuned on the reference. For new flood water: 96% precision and 28% recall (IoU 0.275, F1 0.432). For all water on 17 January: 96% precision, 35% recall (IoU 0.34, F1 0.51). What it marks is almost always flood, but it misses most of it, mainly flooded vegetation and shallow water. The NISAR products are early and not fully calibrated. This is a workaround tested on one flood, not a full solution.

What factors did the team consider?

Honesty first. We checked the Moroccan result in two independent ways, and neither is a clean win.

1) Against the SAR Morocco Flood Dataset on Zenodo, on the same 634,522 pixels. The Otsu threshold reached IoU 0.442 (F1 0.613, precision 0.480, recall 0.849). Our U-Net reached IoU 0.256 (F1 0.407, precision 0.502, recall 0.343). On this reference, the threshold wins. The U-Net is stricter: it finds the darkest water and misses medium-dark water (median −19.5 dB for the water it missed, against −23.6 dB for water both methods found). The reference itself was built with Otsu thresholding: 85.1% of its water is darker than the Otsu line, and 95.2% of its non-water is brighter. So it favours the threshold method, and its acquisition dates may not match 8 February.

2) Against a Sentinel-2 water map from NASA HLS, on 14 February 2026, the same day as a Sentinel-1 pass (1,067,448 clear land pixels, sea removed). 99% of the pixels the U-Net marks as water are water in the optical image too (precision 0.988), but it finds only about a third of what the optical image calls water (recall 0.336, IoU 0.335). The simple threshold scores the same (IoU 0.340), so this check shows that what the model finds is real, not that it beats the threshold. It misses the thin river corridor and shallow edges.

We report all of these numbers and don’t call the Moroccan result validated.

We also considered:

False alarms: sea, coast and river banks, handled by the clean-up step. In the time machine, the model still marks 4 to 12 km² of water on dry dates before February; we show this as its false-alarm floor.

Data limits: radar misses water under trees and between buildings, and OpenStreetMap may be incomplete in rural areas, so road counts are a minimum. Road rows in the situation report list whole road segments, so they are longer than the headline road length.

Free tools only, so anyone can reproduce the work.

No overclaiming: every number has a source, and model outputs are called estimates.

Next steps: train on NISAR L-band with labels (L-band sees under vegetation), improve detection of medium-dark water and thin rivers, score against an expert flood map of Morocco when one becomes available, run automatically when a new satellite pass arrives, and extend the pipeline to other disasters such as landslides and wildfires once labelled data exists.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did we use?

Language: Python.

Libraries: PyTorch, segmentation_models_pytorch, rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, GeoPandas, osmnx.

Web: HTML, JavaScript, Leaflet, hosted on GitHub Pages.

Computing: Google Colab (training), laptops (CPU), Google Drive for data, GitHub for code.

Data services: NASA ASF DAAC and ASF Vertex, ASF HyP3, NASA Earthdata (HLS), NASA GIBS, Copernicus EMS.

No special hardware: everything ran on laptops and free cloud notebooks.
